`HttpResponseBase.__init__` takes optional arguments for a content type, a status, a reason, a charset and a dictionary of headers, and from them sets everything about a response except its content (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.__init__`).

The **reason phrase**, the words after the number on the status line, is normally not stored at all: `HttpResponseBase.reason_phrase` is a property that looks the status code up in Python's table of standard phrases each time it is read, so a response whose status is changed after it was made gets the right words (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.reason_phrase`).

It leaves `HttpResponseBase._handler_class` at `None`; the WSGI or ASGI handler sets it to its own class when the chain hands the response back, so that `HttpResponseBase.close` can name that class as the sender of `request_finished` (`django/core/handlers/wsgi.py:WSGIHandler.__call__`, `django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.run_get_response`, `django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.close`).

`ResponseHeaders` is built on the same `CaseInsensitiveMapping` as a request's `HttpHeaders`, and adds what that read-only class lacks: assignment, deletion, `pop` and `setdefault` (`django/http/response.py:ResponseHeaders`).

`response.headers["Vary"]` and `response["Vary"]` are the same entry, and a membership test, a deletion, `get`, `items` and `setdefault` on a response all mean its headers (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.__setitem__`).

A header that should carry several values, such as `"Vary"`, has to be built up as one comma-separated string; that is what the helpers that patch such headers do (`django/utils/cache.py:patch_vary_headers`, in [Cache headers and conditional requests: `django/utils/cache.py`](../services/http-caching.md)).

A header that should carry several values, such as `"Vary"`, has to be built up as one comma-separated string; that is what the helpers that patch such headers do (`django/utils/cache.py:patch_vary_headers`, in [Cache headers and conditional requests: `django/utils/cache.py`](../services/http-caching.md)).
Every value goes through `ResponseHeaders.__setitem__`, which makes it fit to be sent or refuses it (`django/http/response.py:ResponseHeaders._convert_to_charset`).
A reason phrase is held to a stricter rule by its setter, which since 6.1 refuses any control character (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.reason_phrase`).
The second is read from the header every time and not stored, deliberately, so that a `Content-Type` replaced later takes its charset with it (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.charset`).

Content is encoded in one place, `HttpResponseBase.make_bytes`, through which every piece of it passes: bytes are kept, a string is encoded with the charset, and anything else is turned into a string first (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.make_bytes`).

If what was assigned can be iterated and is not a string, bytes or a `memoryview`, it is consumed there and then, each item converted and all of them joined, and closed if it has a `close`: an `HttpResponse` always holds its whole body, which is what lets a middleware read `content`, measure it or compress it, and what makes the response safe to iterate more than once (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponse.content`).

An `HttpResponse` sets no `Content-Length` of its own: `CommonMiddleware` adds one on the way out, from the length of `content`, if none is set (`django/middleware/common.py:CommonMiddleware.process_response`).

Leaving the body out of what is sent is the server's work, which Django's development server does for itself; the test client does it too, in `conditional_content_removal`, before a test sees the response (`django/core/servers/basehttp.py:ServerHandler.finish_response`, `django/test/client.py:conditional_content_removal`).

A response whose `text` has been read and which is then written to goes on reporting the old text: made with `"one"`, read, and written to with `" two"`, a response holds `b'one two'` and its `text` is still `'one'`, until `content` is assigned again (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponse.text`, `django/http/response.py:HttpResponse.write`).

Several of the response classes are `HttpResponse` with a different `status_code` and nothing else, a class statement with one attribute; the others add a little (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseNotModified`, `django/http/response.py:HttpResponseNotAllowed`).

`HttpResponseRedirectBase.__init__` takes the target first, sets it as `"Location"` after escaping it into ASCII, and then makes two checks (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseRedirectBase.__init__`).

That is a separate question with a separate function, `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme` ([The helpers in `django/utils/http.py`](helpers.md#urls-that-came-from-a-client-url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme)).

Its constructor serialises the data with `json.dumps`, using `DjangoJSONEncoder` unless it is given another encoder, a class that also knows dates, times, decimals and UUIDs; it sets the content type to `"application/json"` unless given a `content_type`; and it hands the result to `HttpResponse` as the body (`django/http/response.py:JsonResponse.__init__`, `django/core/serializers/json.py:DjangoJSONEncoder`).

`JsonResponse` used to refuse anything but a dictionary unless it was called with `safe=False`, as a guard against an attack on a JSON array through JavaScript's array prototype, which the release notes say ECMAScript 5 closed (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).
